title: New F-1 Student — Getting Settled Checklist
intro: A starting checklist for your first weeks in the U.S. Rule-based items link to an official source; logistics items are general guidance — confirm anything about your status with your DSO / international student office.

sections.category: FIRST, right after you land: complete your school's check-in

items.text: Report to your school's Designated School Official (DSO) and complete your school's mandatory immigration check-in so the DSO can finish your initial SEVIS registration (generally within 30 days of your I-20 start date). Until this is done, your record isn't active for the term.

Your specific school sets its OWN required check-in forms, deadlines, and documents — usually completed before or right after orientation. Find and follow YOUR international student office's official website; the exact form differs by school and this checklist can't replace it.
Make sure your I-901 SEVIS fee is paid and have a U.S. physical address ready to give your DSO — SEVIS won't register an Initial-status record without both.
Bring your passport, F-1 visa stamp, Form I-20, and I-94 to check-in.
Keep your passport, F-1 visa stamp, most recent Form I-20, and I-94 record valid and stored safely (digital + paper copies).
Confirm with your DSO that your SEVIS record is 'Active' after you arrive and enroll.
Know your on-campus work limit: up to 20 hours/week while school is in session, full-time during official breaks. No separate work permit needed for on-campus work.
Maintain a full course load every term — dropping below full-time without prior DSO authorization can break your status.
Even if you earn no U.S. income, you generally must file Form 8843 for each year you are an exempt individual.
Learn your tax residency: F-1 students are usually 'exempt individuals' (nonresident) for their first 5 calendar years, which affects which return you file.
If you work, you're generally exempt from Social Security/Medicare (FICA) tax while a nonresident — check your paystub so it isn't withheld in error.
Open a U.S. checking account (most students bring passport, I-20, and proof of address). Ask about no-fee student accounts.
When sending money home, compare the total cost (fees + exchange-rate margin); you have disclosure, cancellation, and error-resolution rights.
Start building a simple monthly budget for rent, food, phone, transport, and health insurance.
Save your DSO / international student office contact and your academic advisor's contact — you'll need both often.
Complete enrollment, get your student ID, and confirm your health insurance is active.
Attend international-student orientation — it usually covers status, work, and tax basics specific to your school.
